rows.title: Calls
rows.text: If you are a big brown bat, you send out 5 to 10 search calls a second, each up to 15 to 20 milliseconds long. If you are a Mexican free-tailed bat, you send out about 4 a second, each about 14 milliseconds long. Nobody has measured the search calls of most other bats, so for them these figures are unknown.
rows.note: Left out R1, R3, R4 (other measured species, but about resolution, range and beam width, not call timing) and R8 (a g record for a different species).

rows.title: Distance
rows.text: If you are a Kuhl's pipistrelle, a calculation from your measured call levels puts the distance at which you can detect an insect at a few meters. For Eptesicus bottae, an open-air hunter, an estimate from field recordings gives about 20 meters for large objects. For most other bats, nobody has measured how far you can detect things.
rows.note: Dropped the word "reports" and my unsupported opening line. R3's quote is cut off, so I used "a few meters" and left out the other threshold ranges. R8 is an estimate for Eptesicus bottae only.

rows.title: Reach
rows.text: An insect a few meters away is about as far as a Kuhl's pipistrelle can detect by echo, according to a calculation from its measured calls. A review gives an estimate of about 20 meters for large objects in Eptesicus bottae, a bat that hunts in open air. If you are another species, nobody has measured how far away you detect things by echo.
rows.note: R3's value text (20 dB SPL) and its quote (the higher threshold) disagree, so I gave only "a few meters" (the quote spans 2 to 7 m for Kuhl's pipistrelle). The Eptesicus bottae figure is an estimate and stays with that species.

rows.title: Direction
rows.text: If you are a pale spear-nosed bat, your echolocation cannot separate two directions that are closer together than about 8 degrees, which is roughly four human thumbs held side by side at arm's length. In bats that call through the mouth, the beam of sound narrows when the bat enters a confined space and widens within dozens of milliseconds when it flies toward open space. Nobody has measured how finely you can tell where an echo comes from unless you are that one species.
rows.note: R1's quote shows "80" where the degree sign was lost; I used the record's value of 8 degrees. Beam-width records for Daubenton's bat (R4) describe the call, not direction resolution, so I left them out.

rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: Every bat measured so far sees far less fine detail than a human, who reads about 30 cycles a degree on an eye chart. If you are a brown big-eared bat, a table compiled from earlier studies lists about 1 cycle a degree, and if you are a great fruit-eating bat, a count of the cells in your retina gives about 2. For most other bats, nobody has measured how sharply you see.

cites.taxon: Artibeus lituratus; A. planirostris; A. obscurus

rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists". Left out other species' figures (vampire bat, Daubenton's bat, etc.) for length, and the big brown bat's R16 because its row grade is i.

rows.title: Dim light
rows.text: If you are a Daubenton's bat, you can detect a round target 10 centimeters across in very dim light, as measured by testing whether bats found it. If you are another Myotis, a close relative of Daubenton's bat, you very likely see in dim light in a similar way. For bats of other groups, nobody has measured how dim a light you can see by.
rows.note: Left out R2 (big brown bat): its value is truncated and the quote gives no light level, so it supports no claim. Left out the threshold number because no record gives a human figure to compare.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: In two bats, Glossophaga soricina and Carollia perspicillata, researchers found two kinds of color-sensing cell in the eye. In eight bat species, a pigment made in the lab sensed ultraviolet light, which humans cannot see. Nobody has measured the color-sensing cells of most bats, so nobody knows how many kinds you have.
rows.note: R2 does not name the eight species in the quote, so the row does not say which they are; the 357 to 359 nm figure was left out as it has no job.

rows.title: Echoes
rows.text: If you are a big brown bat, your search calls go out 5 to 10 times a second, and each one lasts up to 15 or 20 thousandths of a second. If you are a Mexican free-tailed bat, you call about 4 times a second, with each call lasting about 14 thousandths of a second. For most other bats, nobody has measured how you use your calls.
rows.note: Left out R1 (its quote shows "80", the value says 8 degrees), R3 (range depends on threshold), and R6, R7 (group-level beam findings with no named species list).

rows.title: Magnetic compass
rows.text: Imagine flying home across dark country with a compass that needs setting at sunset. If you are a greater mouse-eared bat, you use a magnetic compass, and you calibrate it with cues from the sky at sunset. Nobody has measured whether other bats sense the magnetic field at all.
rows.note: Only R1 (Myotis myotis) supports this row; the other species stay unmeasured, so I stated that plainly and gave no numbers.
